utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour; good morning everyone. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Good morning, Mr. Scott. Good morning, Mr. Mundis. Good morning, Witness. My greetings to the Defence counsel and to the accused. I can see that Mr. Pusic is now with us. We are going to proceed with the examination-in-chief. You have the floor, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Lieutenant Colonel Mr. Birger.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have wrong here, it's Serbo-Croatian, it's not English, and I now with ....

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yesterday when we broke, sir, we were talking about the diary that had been produced by, I believe you said your operations officer, and was completed after you returned to Sweden. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please turn in the bundle that you have now in front of you to the document that's been tabbed 2980. This is P 02980.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it's translated to English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes. And if you go past the English I believe you'll find the document in the original language. Perhaps after page 24 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this document is or this is an extract of a document. Can you tell us what this is, please?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is -- when we was down in Bosnia, every day we was written down what we were doing. If we send out the patrol, we written down when it leave the camp, written down what they do outside, what they're reporting, what -- when they came back, which order I gave to my soldiers and everything what we was involved in, what we do. Everything was written down in paper, minutes, hours, and so on. And at the same time when we was down there my operational officer was summarying every day as a memory for me and my officers and my soldiers, and this paper we have now here looking is this summary. We could call it a diary what we were doing in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. And just so that everyone is clear, sir, when was this diary -- this version of this diary actually created?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was when we was down there. He start creating in winter 1993, 1994, but he finish it when we was back in Sweden and when he was finished I also read it and -- and said okay and then we -- we was ready with it. But it was still ready when we was in Sweden, back in Sweden.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the information that is contained in this diary, when was that information recorded?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was from a paper what we was written down every day what we were doing, and it's -- it was, let's say, a summary. He take the most important thing from every day and written down in this diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let me ask you this: During the time that the 8th Mechanised Company of NordBat was deployed under your command, did you at any point in time receive any written documents from any officers or officials of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I can remember we have -- when I said yesterday we was up in Bobovac Brigade the evening of 23rd -- 24th, sorry, and talking to them about the situation in Stupni Do and especially at the schools or inside the schools, and he -- the Bobovac Brigade commander, now it was changed so it was operational officer so to say was the commander, and he tell me that if you don't take inside all your soldiers to your camp we are going to destroy them. And we have a message later at my gate in the same -- he was with them, the same, take inside your soldiers or we are going to destroy them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you turn, sir, to the document that's been marked as 6103, P 06103. Have you seen this document before, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen that. And the first thing they do we was laughing because we have no signals to anybody about when we was down there. So we don't really understand what -- why they send this message, and we don't do any signals. And so we read it and it was nothing for us to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, how this document was delivered to you?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in the same way as somebody leave it to my soldiers at my company at the gate at my camp, and when I have it to my staff tent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you turn now, sir, to the document that's marked 6151, P 06151.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Birger, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the same type of -- of document, and here you also can see which sign it. If was the former operational officer and now he was the company -- brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And was is this -- this letter in reference to? Why was this letter delivered to you?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- I don't really now -- remember it now, but they don't like us to be out in -- they have to try some control. So we was -- we was out and observed a lots of things, and I don't think they like that. So I -- it was best for them to -- I mean Bobovac Brigade, to have us inside, especially night-time, I think, inside my camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In the first paragraph of this letter, sir, there's again reference to light signals. Do you know what that is in reference to?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know why they was written that. We don't understand that. I remember I talked to them about them -- that and I explained to them we don't see any signals, and I don't know. It could be night-time. We was UN force, so we was -- in order, we have to have a light on the UN flag the whole night so we could -- so we could show what we were -- belonged to the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you turn now, sir, to the document marked 6063. That's P 06063.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: 6063. It should be towards the front part of the binder.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Birger, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I remember that this also arrived. Maybe I don't really know which way it came, if it came from our fax or it came to our gate, but it was order to -- to the Bobovac Brigade that cooperates with UNPROFOR and don't shoot against UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you remind us what had occurred on the 24th of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you remind us what had occurred on the 24th of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 24th of October the Bobovac Brigade was shooting at my APCs down in Vares in the evening. Maybe they start about 10.00 at the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, at the -- at the time you received this document, did you know who General Milivoj Petkovic was?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know now, but I think I ask who this was, and maybe I have some answer about who this was, but I never meet him, and I don't know which this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to turn now, sir, and show you a couple of documents relating to Stupni Do. Can you please look at document in your bundle 6218. That's P 06218.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant Colonel Birger, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember I have seen it, but I can see it's sent from -- from our fax up in that page, and who has sign it was Tomas Eriksson, he's the senior medical officer in our battalion staff, and on the right it's Captain Peter Nilson. He was one of my platoon leaders. And I know Peter assistanced this doctor when they was up in Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in looking at this document, sir, can you tell us how this document relates to the information that you received concerning what had happened in Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember we find three women down in the basement shooted in the head and in the breast and maybe that is three of this -- maybe two, six or another earlier. And we also find one man just outside a village. Maybe he'd tried to escape up in the wood. He was shooting in the back, and you could also see his -- we have one here shooting in the back. We also find bodies who was burned. So it's what -- that information we have in the report we was written and sent out, sent to my headquarter, was about 16 bodies, and we have a lot of pictures about it, and so I think it's -- for me it's maybe more or less correct what I -- the information I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you turn, sir, to the next page of this document and perhaps tell us what this sketch map relates to.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about the village of Stupni Do and where we find the bodies, and here also you could see which ways we came into -- into Stupni Do. We start from -- from, so to say, right side, this road, and the 2nd platoon came in from Vares area. And it was -- this place is where we find the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you now turn, sir, to the document again towards the front of the bundle with the number 6049. That's P 06049. Now, Lieutenant Colonel Birger, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really remember, but I could recognise something about it, but I don't remember everything it's so long time ago, but I know we have a lot of letters more or less every evening, couple of days in this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, at the bottom on the left-hand side under the heading "Distribution," can you tell us if you know, sir, what BHC G-5 would refer to?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The BH, it's UNPROFOR's Bosnian command, I can understand, and G-5 is in NATO structure where you're planning or it's liaison section. I think in this way this is liaison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you look, sir, specifically at the third paragraph - excuse me - the third paragraph under the heading "Inform" with the sentence that begins, "I do not have any checked information." Could you read that, please?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't understand why they written like this. I don't understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you elaborate upon what you don't understand?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand that they written "any attacking activities of HVO Vares, so I doubt about the information from Muslim side concerning the master in Stupni Do village." What I can understand, it was HVO who was attacking Stupni Do. They inform that about the morning of the 23rd, and we also observed soldiers from HVO when we enter the village on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Birger, how would you characterise the accuracy of the information in that paragraph that you've just read?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I -- I don't really understand what they have -- maybe -- no, I don't know what to say about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me now show you, sir, approximately three documents concerning the schools in Vares. Can you turn, please, to 6161. This is P 06161. Are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. That is -- I have not -- my deputy was still in -- in Pancevo based in Belgrade, so battalion commander sent down Major Ekberg. He arrived at the morning of 25. So when he came down where he was, so to say, my deputy, and one thing he was -- so we -- we have this plan at -- I talk to Bobovac Brigade. He talked to BH side, so to say. And in this moment we tried the whole time to get inside the school and I couldn't be there the whole time. So when I don't was where, he was there, and this day he could -- we was allowed to get inside the school. So Major Ekberg and also one doctor from our battalion, Mech [phoen], and also one military police and I could also see the interpreter. Glavan [phoen] was a soldier from the 10 Mechanised Company. And they were allowed to get inside and they could on -- also there was they was also allowed to talk so some of the prisoner, and I remember that they tell me that they was very afraid. All was beaten up, some of them very bad. It was -- what we could understand young boys, more or less, who came inside, beaten up, and leave the building again. And in the end he -- I also know he was telling me that he talked to them and said, "Now what -- we know now what's happening here. We know which you are -- which -- in this building. So we are going to everything to help you, so we are going to try to stop this." And what you also can read in Major Ekberg's conclusion is what I just say is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you turn now, sir, to the document marked 6180. P 06180.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you know who Dr. Drazen Grgic is?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you look and focus your attention on paragraph number 4 of this document, and I'd ask you to take a look at paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you comment on what's contained in paragraph -- I'm sorry, this is the very bottom paragraph on the page that starts, "There are no records."

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I have to read it. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, based upon your knowledge and understanding of the situation in Vares in late October 1993, can you comment upon what's written in paragraph 4 of P 06180?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what we should evacuate 150 civilians from Stupni Do. We never do that. Not from Stupni Do. We have a lot of refugees inside Vares, and I also built up a refugee camp just north of my company camp, but we was not up in Stupni Do. We never take care about 100 civilians up in Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about the reference in the final line in the English version of "27 sick and elderly people will be released today"?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which belong to which day it is. 27 of October. The information I had was that we -- when we was inside the school in the last -- the south school in the last day of October it was information that it was 27 prisoner was very bad beaten up, and they wasn't there in the south school. And we tried to find out where they was, and later we have an information what we was down in Vares-Majdan and I was police station, and we also find there I think it was the 3rd of November, but I know -- never know what they have sent them out -- [microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you now look at the next document -- can you -- sir, can you now look at the next document, P 06201. 6201.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again I would ask you to read paragraph 4 which begins, "With the permission of the military authorities." If you could please take a read through that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it was written the 28th of October. Now we have -- we have -- have a visit with 27 elderly and sick Muslim civilians, and what I can understand -- maybe we can call -- it relates. It was not in the south school but it was in another place, and this place we find the 3rd of November down in Vares-Majdan where the 27 prisoner was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you comment about --

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I can -- I could also see I have written they don't beat them up any more, and what I understand after the 25 of -- of October, what we talked to the prisoners, some of them telling us in these days -- after this day they don't beat them up any more, and it was this day we tried to get inside the school with one platoon outside the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how does that relate to the information contained in paragraph 4 of this document?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it's little bit true that they don't beat them up any more. That was -- I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: All right. Lieutenant Colonel Birger, I just have a couple of remaining questions about interaction that you had with officials from the ECMM, the European Commission Monitoring Mission. Do you recall having at any point in time during your deployment meetings or discussions or briefings with ECMM?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not so much. When we came down there was more to say three organisations what talked to the different parts. It was ECMM. It was UNPROFOR, UNMOs, and it was UNPROFOR, so to say, armed forces, and I remember that it could be some problems sometimes, but it was not coordinated. So we could be in the same place, the same time, try to talk to the same commander, so to say. So in UNPROFOR we -- we -- after these days later in this year we have some little -- this little organised. So the UNMOs worked more or less more close together with my battalion, but the ECMM, I had meeting. We meet, and they came to my camp and have some information, leave some information, but I couldn't remember that it was some really cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you turn, sir, to the document marked 6092. That's P 06092. That is ECMM report of 25 October 1993. I would ask you, sir, to turn towards the bottom of this document, approximately 10 or 12 lines from the bottom where there's reference, it says, "Together with UK LO teams B 3 and B 4 visited NordBat in Vares." Can you read that yourself please from that line to the bottom of this document?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I have read it, and I don't really remember what they was there, and they was talking to the Bobovac Brigade, but I remember at the beginning I was in -- in -- in Bosnia. A lot of times it was a United Kingdom liaison team came into my area, talked to us, follow us out -- out in the terrain, and maybe they at us also looking how we do our work, so to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you comment, sir, on the last paragraph that indicates an acceptance of yourself as a mediator between the parties?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that because in these days, what I say, I was negotiation for NordBat to the Bobovac Brigade, and my way, they was it for the BH army. So I -- I have meeting a couple of weeks before we was out in the terrain, and he know me well, and I think now in this situation he was a little bit pressed. He was -- I remember these days he was very nervous, sweating and so on, when I talked to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you, sir -- the duties that you carried out when dealing with the Bobovac Brigade, would you characterise those as being in the role of a mediator?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, we tried to -- to stop firing -- to fighting so we could get into Stupni Do. And if it was exactly these days, I don't know, but in -- before we came in from the 34rd [sic] of October until we came into Stupni Do we tried to stop fighting so we could get inside there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you turn now, sir, to the document -- this is the last document I'll show you, 6117. That's P 06117.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This is a document from the ECMM coordination centre Travnik dated 26 October 1993. Could you turn in the English version, sir, to page 2.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With the paragraph that begins "HCC the head of the coordination centre was briefed in Vares by NordBat." Could you please read --

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Repeat that, where?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the beginning it says HCC was briefed in Vares by NordBat. Could you please read that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yeah. I could read that, and what is written here is more or less what we understand was what's more or less happening in Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you comment on the part that indicates that there had been interviews by Muslims who were evacuated from the outskirts of Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- it was before we get into Stupni Do. I don't remember exactly which day. We have a patrol down -- it was Major Ekberg. He was going down south of Vares to the BH army to negotiate with them, and suddenly when we came up the road it came some refugees down from the wood on the road, and it was also some HVO soldiers with them. And I remember they informed me after this that they have been in the beginning very hardly against the HVO soldier, take the weapon from them and visit them and so on, but this women who was there said, "Don't do anything about them because they was -- this man who will save us out from Stupni Do." And I also remember they talk to them and one of the women don't want to talk to them when they was in, so to say, the BH army headquarters. So after, with the interpreter, she informed by that, that she had been raped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant Colonel Birger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no further questions, and before I sit down I will indicate, as I informed my colleagues from the Defence last evening that, with respect to the remaining exhibits that had been listed for this witness, the Prosecution will not be filing or seeking to adduce any of those additional documents. We will simply tender the 11 documents that we showed the witness this morning, but I just wanted to put that on the record to avoid any confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Now for the Defence. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Good morning to you, Lieutenant Colonel, sir. I will have a couple of questions for you on behalf of the Defence for General Praljak. I won't have too many, I hope. Let's start in the chronological order. There's one thing that struck me. In view of the plans your unit had for its deployment in this area of Bosnia, Kiseljak, Vares, and the local areas, according to these plans it seems that you intended to be there with all the units ready at the start of October 1993. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have all my company in there in the beginning of October. It was only me and recon guy, my platoon leaders, and some more soldiers. If I remember right, it was 10 together with me. And we arrived to Vares area the 1st of October, and my first platoon arrived to the area the 20 of October. And after that, they came day for day and in the 23rd, 24th, in this day I had three platoons. So not the whole company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Correct. It's a fact that you arrived there at the time and that you deployed the way you just described. However, according to the plans, it seems you had intended to be there in the beginning of October with many more forces than you in fact had. In other words, the deployment plans envisaged a much larger force there at the time. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know. It was -- it was one Engineering Company there from a Canadian battalion which, of course, was part of UNPROFOR, but it was not part of NordBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am trying to receive information from you concerning NordBat. In view of the problems you had in Pancevo, and you referred to that in your statement, I am under the impression that your deployment plans were quite late and that around the 20th of October, according to your original plans, all the platoons of your battalion should have been deployed there by that time. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both yes and no. What I remember when we was travelling down to Bosnia from Denmark, we should have maybe two trains per day or something like -- like this down to Pancevo. And when we was travelling down there the Serbian government changed what to one train for two days. So everything was delayed, that is right, but I don't remember exactly. I mean, maybe we could be in there a little bit earlier with one or two platoons, but the plan said -- but reconnaissance team get down and some days later, week later, we start to second down the part of our battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. But in essence can we agree that primarily due to the problems in Pancevo cause by the authorities of the Republic of Serbia, your deployment in this part of Bosnia, Kiseljak, and Vares was delayed because the Serbian authorities had imposed certain restrictions on you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You, and I don't mean you personally but your superior command, decided to change the routes on the way to Bosnia, and you moved your forces to Croatia, to certain bases in Croatia. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, we do, but in -- maybe in some days in November I remember why, because we was in the village of Olovo, and it was shooting against my APCs, and we get down to the -- to the brigade commander in Olovo and talk to them and say, Why are you shooting against my APCs? And he show us the house. It was, he said, the Serbian house. The next time we was there we was firing back, and there after that I came now. After that they stop all APCs came into Bosnia. Before the Serbian government also have stopped the tank from the Danish company. Therefore we change the route and they came into the area in -- in beginning of or middle of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation. However, we are not interested in these events at that time. I should only like you to either confirm this or deny it. I put it to you that, as you say, in the beginning of November you started moving your troops and logistics through Croatia and that on your way through Croatia the Croatian authorities did not impede you in any way to move along to Bosnia together with the panoply of your equipment. Is that true or not? That's all I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can -- I was not involved in the planning of the deployment of the battalion. That was over my level. I was in the area. I was only informed what equipment arrived, when the soldier arrived, when the APCs, other vehicles arrived, and so on. I was not involved in planning. I was not involved to negotiation. It was over my level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. But this will be the last question I have on this topic so that I will not have wasted my time. Did you later on during your stay in Bosnia receive any information along the chain of command that any forces that should have replaced you were late because of possible problems they had experienced in Croatia? Did you ever hear anything to that effect?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said, I was not involved in this planning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that you were, nevertheless, an officer who was placed not too high along the chain of command, but nevertheless as an officer you would have been privy to such information, and did you ever hear that -- of republic -- of the Republic of Croatia ever placing any obstacles to any activities you may have been carrying out in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not what I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You spoke of the preparations in your unit for the deployment to Bosnia, including the joint training with the Danish forces in Denmark. During the training, what was the extent of it -- the information you received concerning the political and military situation and developments in Bosnia-Herzegovina, specifically concerning the area you -- you were supposed to be deployed to? What sort of briefing had you had there?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have -- we have a briefing from -- from a different way. We have from the government side in Sweden. We have information from UNPROFOR down in -- in Zagreb. We have information from the battalions in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We have a lot of information about also the political situation down in -- in Bosnia. What I remember, it was this summer a lot of fighting in -- between Muslims and Croat forces, so to say, in Vitez, Kiseljak. In Tuzla it was more or less little bit calm. It was not fighting areas, and it was, so to say, a good area to be if you don't want to be in -- in fighting. Also in Mostar we see some -- a lot of fighting. When I came -- when I was down there, just before we was down when they inform me what we have to deploy in the village of -- in the city of Vares, and what I could understand the UNPROFOR headquarter in Kiseljak, BH command, was little afraid something was going on in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, I thank you for the information you gave me in response to my question. However, I have to tell you that I am under certain time constraints, and I would like you to answer my questions without any additional explanations. I will ask for further explanations if I will need any. When you arrived in Vares, and of course you had by that time already received certain information, you were the first ones on behalf of NordBat to -- I mean you personally were the first one to have got into contact with the Bobovac Brigade on behalf of NordBat; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could the court deputy pull up 3D 00854. And we could turn to page 4 of the document, please. That's 0313. I will show you a document used by the British forces for their briefings. You should have it in your -- oh, no. It hasn't shown up yet. We'll have to wait a bit.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which number again? 3 -- 03 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] In this folder in front of you. I will ask you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, you have it on the screen now. I need page 0313, and I believe you moved ahead. 0313. That's page 4, including the cover page. I would like to refer you to one passage. This page contains the basic information about the HVO. That's under the heading "Armed forces." Please read the first paragraph as well as the second one. You have it on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] It's the last document in the bundle. [In English] Last document in the bundle, sir. Last document in the bundle. And it is page 3 or 4.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So I'm kindly asking you to read the first two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant Colonel --

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This description of the HVO and the relevant municipalities, does it correspond in its basic outline to what your impressions were of the Bobovac Brigade as you arrived there up until the start of the conflict? Would you agree with the assessment given here?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really that way, but Bobovac Brigade inform us. It was Emil Harah or something like this who was the brigade commander, and another person was the mayor of Vares. It was not the same person. But I never read that, and I -- I -- the information I have written down informing the statement, what my -- the information I have about the situation, who was the leaders and so on, that was the information was given from the HVO to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On the basis of some of your notes, would you agree that the Bobovac Brigade and the political leadership of the Vares municipality were quite close and cooperated closely, that the Bobovac Brigade basically belonged to Vares municipality? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Belong and belong -- we was working to the, yes. It was more or less together, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I am not going into what the situation was after the 23rd, after the conflict at Stupni Do, because after this conflict the situation somewhat changed, admittedly. Let's move on. Is it true that at the time of your arrival in Vares there were no conflicts there between the HVO and the BH army? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes and no. What I can understand it was no fighting against HVO and the 2nd Corps, what's mean the Tuzla Corps from BH army and the brigade in Olovo and so on. They more or less little bit cooperating, but in the west, about the 3rd Corps, it was definitely not friendly. It was fighting there, and I remember one day we was out where I have to take cover because they also shot against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I thank you for your answer. However, my question had to do with Vares municipality, because Olovo that you refer to is outside that municipality. Would you agree with me that in Vares municipality there were -- there was no active fighting between the two factions we just referred to?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, but also --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But also the civilian municipality in my opinion was more -- had had more together with the Serbian side or what they have with the BH side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you think that this might have affected the relations between the municipal political structure and the Bobovac Brigade leadership, because this is what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Since you yourself mentioned that there were certain relations with the Serb side, my question is: Do you believe that this might have in any way affected the relations between the municipal HVO unit and the Vares political leadership? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was both, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You wouldn't know in which way these would have a bearing?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- what I could understand, they have oil and the logistics and so on through the Serbian side. That mean what I can understand they use the road for to -- from Kiseljak, for example, to Vares it was via Serbian side, Serbian territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Of course you were quite aware of the fact that Vares municipality was in full encirclement and did not have any physical contact with the other territories in Bosnia under the HVO control; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know what you mean about that, because when I talk in the military way I understand the 2nd Corps in Tuzla said it was a part of this corps, but the Bobovac Brigade said no, they was not involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, my question is a simple one. That's why by way of an introduction I asked you about your preparations and what units you had in Bosnia. Is there any doubt, sir, that the area of Vares municipality, including Kiseljak, was in full encirclement and had no contacts with the other territories in Bosnia-Herzegovina that were under the HVO control, because they were surrounded by either the BH army units or Republika Srpska army? I believe this is a notorious fact, a fact of common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this could be like this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Before, you will agree with me that they had to receive supplies from somewhere because they would have starved a year earlier if this had not been the case. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Line 23 of the transcript does not reflect the witness's answer, and I believe the witness said that he could agree with what I said.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You have just mentioned the view of the 2nd Corps which differed from that of the Bobovac Brigade command. Can the witness be shown 3D 00841. 3D 00841. We will not be referring to your statement or the diary or the logbook of your unit. I would like to ask you the following: Do you agree that the direct conflicts between the BH army and the HVO in the territory of Vares municipality started on or about the 18th of October when the army attacked Kopjari? Can you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The real -- the attack to take control over Kopjari start later, but it was fighting in the area both in Kopjari, Bojovic, and Sladin [phoen], Planinica, that mean the south-west part of area in these days, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the first conflicts broke out as early as on the 8th -- or, sorry, the 11th of October, the first skirmishes? I should perhaps read it out from your statement -- or, rather, logbook concerning the 11th of October. That's the logbook belonging to your unit.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said so in my statement. That's correct. I don't remember it now, it's many years ago, but I remember it was small so to say fighting in October, before the 21st of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. For the transcript, this is P 0298. But I do agree with what you're saying, Lieutenant Colonel. However, the logbook of your unit, the entry for the 11th of October, states in the last line of that paragraph: "'In today's morning briefing,' the battalion commander said," and this is inverted commas, "'that shells are raining on Vares.'"? Now, if he's saying this then obviously there was some sort of an attack mounted on Vares. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was -- that's not correct. It was correct what was written in the diary because we have a radio. We have a radio so we could hear the news from Sweden. In Sweden they said, in the news they said that the battalion commander has -- their effect to the commander, and said it was -- there are impacts in Vares and we was laughing because we said that is not correct because we are here and there was no impact inside Vares on this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us go back to Kopjari. You saw certain signs of rising tensions before the real conflict broke out, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. We -- we understand what something going on in this area, in Kopjari area, and it was also therefore I immediately the first -- my Alpha platoon, when this arrived, I immediately take it up to this area, and they was there in the last afternoon, the 20 of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Lieutenant Colonel, from this document, and it's brief written by the assistant commander of the 2nd Corps of the BH, he says that in Kosare [phoen] inspecting units of operation group 3 on the 18th of October, 1993, at 6.30, he got information from the Bobovac unit that the operative units and the 3rd Corps for Kakanj in Breza on the 17th of October at 1930 hours, they attacked the Bobovac Brigade in Lijesnica, Kopjari, Plijesac? You have spoken about this. Do you agree this information is correct? It corresponds to the knowledge that you had?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. My next question in this connection. I do have to read another bit I'm skipping a paragraph. The same commander writes: "Units of the 3rd Corps attacked the Bobovac Brigade without any provocation whatsoever and thus threatened the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Corps. I demand that you immediately order the commander of the 3rd Corps to halt the above-mentioned action and to return the units of the 3rd Corps that participated in the attack to their initial positions." We saw from your notes that there were units of the 3rd Corps and units of the 2nd Corps of the BH army in that location. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we start in -- south of Vares we were -- in this stage we was not really sure which corps it was in the south, but I think we -- we -- in our opinion it was the 6th Corps, but we was very sure what in west, so to say, it was the 3rd Corps. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you knew that elsewhere there is another corps with which the Bobovac Brigade was cooperating?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the 2nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As time went on, and we see entries about that in your diary, you found out there was the 7th Muslim Brigade active within the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Please just answer with a yes or no. It will proceed more quickly. We'll go step-by-step. Will you agree that in that brigade or some smaller other groups within the 3rd Corps there were units that many participants in the war referred to as the Mujahedin? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never meet any Mujahedin, no. But I meet the 7 Muslim brigade, yes, in Vares. But if there were any Mujahedin inside or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Would you agree with me -- rather, let me rephrase this. Did you observe in that period and in later months that there is a major difference in the conduct and attitude between the 2nd and the 3rd Corps of the BH army? Were you able to observe that?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You, as trained professional soldier, didn't you find it at least odd that two corps level, strong units that should presumably be under the same command acted quite differently? Wasn't that a bit strange?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe. There was a lot of thing for me who was very -- I don't understand a lot of thing when I came down there. It was very, very bad situation we have in the Vares area. So who was command under who was one of the biggest question we have to try to find out in the first weeks. But I -- in my understand it was under the same command. I mean, the 2nd Corps, the 3rd Corps was a part of BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We saw, actually, an example of the major problems they had between them. Let me remind you, in one paragraph of your statement, and even in the diary, you mentioned that at one point after Stupni Do the 2nd Corps of the BH army asked you, the UNPROFOR, to somehow control the separation between the areas covered by the 2nd Corps and the 3rd Corps respectively, that you refused. Do you agree with that? You seem to be nodding but I need an answer for the record.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved in this negotiation but I know my battalion commander was involved in the negotiation with the 2nd Corps and they asked them to be, so to say, a part of -- between these two corps. That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And now I'm coming back to my earlier question. You are a professional, trained soldier. You told me that the situation was very confusing, and you were wondering who was answerable to whom. Wasn't that a clear warning to you that something is wrong there? Those were seemingly two units of the same army but they didn't seem to be the same army. Did you have any doubts about that? Did you find an answer?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, in this situation I was not thinking so much about that because we have a lot of thing to do. We have also to bring built up my so to say camp. It was very, very bad situation for my company. So I don't -- I was not thinking in this way but, of course, it was a little bit, so to say, crazy situation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But if we can save some time, can we agree that you did observe that even on the HVO side there were units controlled by superior command and other units that are not real little controlled by the superior command? Can you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say like this: I know the different parts, the Muslims, the Serbs, and the Croats' army have parts of units who do bad things, but I also know that they use them in the way what we have to do. They was more or less under control. So if they don't want to have them to do what they do, they could stop them. I -- In my opinion they use these type of forces for their own aim. I mean, the BH army used the 7 Muslim Brigade because they know it was a little bit tough for soldiers to get into Stupni Do. I also know that -- that in the same way it was in the Serbian army we meet them later soldiers, so to say, or more or less criminals who do bad things against me and my soldiers. And also in the Bobovac Brigade it was the same type this soldiers or terrorist or criminals, what you can call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That seems to be a general assessment. But precisely in that kind of environment you were objectively unable to establish at what point within one period some units or individuals or, let's say, groups are not under the control of any one command. You simply had no basis to determine that. Would you agree were me?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I -- I'm -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No. No will do. Thank you very much. I'll describe a situation, and you will try to clarify. You mentioned one minor incident near a tunnel by the check-point where there is a roundabout route to Stupni Do. They didn't want to let you through. There were negotiations going on, discussions, and then a group showed up, and when they went away the guard at the check-point said they are crazy, and then somebody answered, "If they are crazy, why are you not arresting them?" You were personally involved in at least one such situation. My question is this: That group that showed up, that was going from one place to another, and they were all armed, were you able to -- to determine that they fit anywhere at all within the chain of command? Were they under anybody's command, or were they just an independent group that was taking advantage of the reigning chaos for their own material gain? Based on those circumstances and everything you knew at that time, were you able to say, "Yes, I know that this group is answerable to somebody, reports to somebody"?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. In my opinion, in the 33rd [sic] of October it was a little bit chain of command in the Bobovac Brigade, and this, so to say, soldiers who was there that you describe at the tunnel where there was at this moment a part under the command of a new leadership in Bobovac Brigade. The policemen was afraid about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't think we really understood each other. Maybe I wasn't clear enough. Regardless of the change in the leadership of the Bobovac Brigade, the soldiers and the policemen who were full time stationed at the check-point were under somebody's command, and they must have been under the command of the Bobovac Brigade because it was the municipal brigade in the area. But that group that showed up at the moment when you were there, who were menacing and who were called crazy by the guard at the check-point, I'm asking you about them. They came, threatened, left, and you had a short discussion about them with the police detail at the check-point. At that moment, based on those specific circumstances and everything you knew about how things work in Bosnia, were you able to conclude that those people were under somebody's command, or, and we have only two choices, you decided that they were looters, robbers, who were taking advantage of the chaos to get rich in the war? Was it clear to you that they were somebody's men? Was it reasonably clear?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I understand Ivica Rajic was coming the 33rd [sic] of October to the area. Some days before we have observed, so to say, soldiers in the same what you have described here, these type of soldiers. So it was new soldiers who arrived to the area, and it was also these soldiers here at the tunnel. But it was also clear to me that they were under command of the Bobovac Brigade but they have changed command. It was very clear, because they, the Bobovac Brigade, pointed out for us, "You are not allowed to go up to Stupni Do." They do everything to stop us. "You are not allowed to be out in your positions night-time. You must go inside." And this after that they have said so the first time. There was also shooting against us the night of 24th of October. So for me it was very clear what everything was going on was under the command of the Bobovac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, Witness, this small group of looters, let's call them, did they have any insignia, what kind of uniforms they wore?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They have more -- they have more -- course, it was crosses. And of course in the hair and so on, they have no hair. They could shave it off. Some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That was something chose be by them individually, but did you notice the insignia on their uniforms that signified an affiliation to something?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the whole situation in Bosnia it was not so often you could see they have a uniform. You could see what they belonged to. Also in this day the Bobovac Brigade, just before Vares was taken by the BH army, they use band of right -- left arm here so they could show that they belonged to which side. They were not a clear uniform so you could say which side or so to say which unit they belong. That's correct, no uniform in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let us be quite clear because we have touched upon the issue of uniforms quite a few times here. To sum up, if I understood you correctly, the uniform without a patch was absolutely no sign of affiliation to any army as a general principle. All armies used various kinds of uniforms. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was various. It was -- normally we also saw a lot of shirts with the German flag and so on. So it was a lot of mixed clothes and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Since you have mentioned German insignia, I believe that if you saw a shirt with the German flag on the sleeve you would not conclude that the soldiers wearing it were German, would you?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The next distinctive sign was some kind of badges that troops wore on the chest or sometimes on the sleeve. I'm interested particularly in the HVO. Those badges were different. The initiated could distinguish between members of various units on the basis of these badges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you have used 45 minutes so far, and you were allowed to use up 30 minutes. I imagine that other lawyers or other Defence counsels gave you their time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We have enough time, and I think most of the time will be used between Ms. Alaburic and myself, and if some time is left Mr. Praljak will have a few questions using a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just to conclude, Witness, let me go back to that group. If it's true that you didn't see any distinctive signs on them, you were unable to tell who they belonged to just on the basis of their uniform; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember how exactly -- which clothes they have. It's more than 10 years ago. And -- but it's very clear for me what they belonged to the Bobovac Brigade or the leadership of the -- the new leadership. Bobovac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Witness. My client will ask you a few questions himself. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]. Good morning. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. I would like to place a map by Mr. Birger. And while that is being done, let me ask you this: From all you know, were there elements of civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did that conflict include certain elements of civil war? From everything you know from history or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Praljak. I think that's not the correct question because it asks for a legal qualification, which the witness is not qualified to give. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Never mind then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You said you had not seen a single Mujahedin. Did your superiors inform you of the existence of Mujahedin in the 3rd Corps and their number? Did you have such information?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have some information that it was what you call Muslim elements in -- in the 3rd Corps, and also information about it was very hardly [sic] corps, and we have also example for that in the village of Borovica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I am sincerely surprised by your references to some information, certain knowledge, et cetera. You were soldiers. I'm sure that you had pretty good briefings. Anyway, you have a map behind you which depicts the development of movements of the 3rd and later 2nd Corps against Vares. The map was developed based on your diary and some information you have already shared with us. Could you please look at the map and tell us whether it is accurate. And if you don't think it's accurate, could you tell us in which way. The colour green shows the advance of the Muslims, the fall of various villages as described in your diary until their entry into Vares, and on the right-hand side the pull-out of the HVO, the refugees towards Dastansko, and the areas controlled by the army of Republika Srpska. Is this military map accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm asking the technicians whether it's possible to let us share the view of the map, because at this distance without the optical instrument necessary we cannot see it. Maybe a camera could -- yes. That's already better. Maybe it can be a bit sharper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can explain little. What I can see -- what I can -- it's not working. What I can see here on the map, it should be the 3rd Corps who was attacking up in Dubostica and in Vijaka. In my opinion, it was wrong; it was forces from the 2nd Corps, and it was forces from the 3rd Corps up in the line like this, north of Borovica and south, in this direction. Here it was forces from the 2nd Corps who was attacking the pocket of Vares. That seems correct here down, think it was attacking in this direction. It was also correct that were, so to say, the rest of Bobovac Brigade escaped to the village of Dastansko in this area here and they would stay here after it had been a little bit calmed down in the area. So it's more or less here up. I don't think it's really correct, in my opinion, about it, what we understand. It was the 3rd Corps, the 3rd Operational Group from a third -- from a second corps who attack and take Dubostica and Pogar. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I just want to make one thing clear. Do you know that Krivaja river depicted in the upper part of the map separated the 3rd from the 2nd Corps? Do you know that Krivaja river was the separation line between the 2nd and the 3rd Corps? Therefore, this map depicts the position of the 2nd Corps completely correctly as attacking Vijaka village? If you know these two things, that Krivaja was the separation line between the 2nd and the 3rd Corps, and indeed it is indicated that the 2nd Corps was attacking Vici or Vijaka village, then it is quite accurately depicted on the map that these various components attacked these villages.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say it again. It was the 2nd Corps who was attacking in this area in Pogar, Vijaka, and also the representatives of the 2nd Corps. The command of the 3rd OG, they have their responsibility for various area. Later they change. They changed command. They changed forces inside Vares area. It was sometimes I understand it was from the 3rd Corps, but in the end of my time in -- at the month of April, the Vares area and so on was the part of the 1st Corps, 1st Corps. But I don't really know what -- I can understand where --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, please. Please. I'm asking you kindly. We're talking about the fall of Vares. We're not talking about April 1994. I'm asking you nicely. Tell me, if you think this map is inaccurate, how is it inaccurate? Take a pencil and say, "I think the map is inaccurately depicting this. I don't think the 3rd Corps was there. I think the 2nd corps was there instead." Leave the -- April 1994 alone. Please take a pencil and tell me, "Mr. Praljak, it's incorrect in this and that spot for this and that reason."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution objects, Your Honour. We have given both the Praljak Defence team and General Praljak some leeway here. But really we've gone well beyond context in terms of what might be admissable. This is generally, this is irrelevant to the charges listed in the indictment. The Vares municipality charges certainly are much more narrow than any of this evidence that General Praljak is seeking to educe and this is, with all due respect, not a productive use of the Trial Chamber's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, you have a map before you. The Defence is showing you this map. From where I'm sitting, but I was able to see the map on the screen, it would seem that the Vares area was circled by the BiH army except at the bottom where we see that the VRS is holding the position at the bottom. Now, the Defence, or General Praljak, is telling you that it's the 3rd Corps that was attacking or that was making this operation on Vares. You see the 2nd Corps, the 3rd Corps. Except for the mention of the 2nd Corps to the right where you can see 2nd Corps. Now, this being said, do you agree with the lines the way they were drafted here, and independently of the lines the fact that there is a mention of a 3rd Corps and a 2nd Corps, is that placed where they really were placed at the time? And this is with regard to the period covering the end of October, early November, since the dates that General Praljak is mentioning go from the 18th to the 22nd of October. It's Pogar, and they also go to the 3rd of November. So now, there you are. You were there. Only you can tell us what the situation was like. You were a neutral party, and you can tell us if this map is correct, if it's not correct. And if I understood you correctly, I thought General Praljak wanted you to tell us why you don't agree with this map and what is erroneous with this map and what does not correspond to what you saw on the field when you were deployed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. That's both the 3rd Corps and the 2nd Corps who get inside Vares. 2nd Corps more or less from east and the north, and the 3rd Corps from west and south. The only thing I don't agree with the map was up in Dubostica, Pogar area. I said that was the 2nd Corps was attacked. The situation in Vares area with these both corps is correct in this days we are talking about. They came into Vares from different -- from north and south, so to say. That's correct. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you please mark next to Dubostica, can you please mark that spot and write the 2nd Corps. And can you then please sign map and place today's date on it.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say I couldn't do that exactly. That's impossibility of two reasons. It's a long time ago, and we don't have that exact information. I could only talk about village. What I know, the village of Dubostica was taken by the 2nd corps, the 3rd Operational Group, because we meet the commander there at the evening when it was taken. We also could see they have prisoners from HVO there [Realtime transcript read in error "from there"], prisoner of war. We also know that the village of Pogar was taken by the 2nd Corps because I meet the Chief of Staff of the corps up in Pogar which day it was taken. But exactly where the border between these two corps was in the terrain, I couldn't mark out. I could only talking about village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, you told us that Dubostica and Pogar were taken by the 2nd Corps. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, yes. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Could you please circle Dubostica. Put a circle around Dubostica and write 2nd Corps next to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting the examination, but I see that there's one sentence uttered by the witness that was not reflected in the record. The witness said that when he met at Dubostica with the representatives of the 2nd Corps that he saw HVO prisoners of war there, and this sentence was left out of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the witness repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can repeat it, and it was not my person. It was my deputy commander who was there and he reporting to me. It was about 20, 25 prisoner of war HVO soldiers in Dubostica. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask Their Honours to permit the witness to sign the -- and place the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please put on the map Dubostica and Pogar and please write down 2nd Corps because this is what you told us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks] THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you write "The 2nd Corps," please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you remember, could you please mark 2nd Corps around the two circles, because the witness told us it was 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, you drew two circles. Now, these two circles, do they correspond to the 2nd Corps? If so, then please just mark under the circles, 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The circle is the two village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well. Could you please give us a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this map will become Exhibit IC 510.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is 10.40. We'll take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak, how much time do you need to complete your questions? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, several minutes. I only have a couple of questions left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few minutes. That could mean one hour, because one hour is 60 minutes. You are talking about several minutes. What does it mean? Ms. Alaburic, you gave us your binder. How much time would you need, Ms. Alaburic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the other Defence teams gave their time to me, and should you deem my cross-examination relevant for the case, I hope that I will be allowed to examine the witness until the close of business today -- or, rather, I can leave sufficient time for re-examination and Judges' questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I understand correctly, there won't be any questions on behalf of Mr. Prlic, neither for Mr. Stojic, Mr. Pusic neither, and neither for Mr. Coric. Therefore, we have a cross-examination that will be conducted only for and by Generals Praljak and Petkovic. Please proceed, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In your statement given on the 6th and the 7th of February, 2001, on page 3 in the Croatian version you speak of the 21st of October, 1993, and on page 4 you say the following concerning this date: "I left Kopjari around 1700 hours. As I was leaving, the commander of the BH army on the ground called out to me and said, 'See you in Vares.' On our way I saw some soldiers of the BH army herding sheep from Kopjari to Dragovici." Is it true that this is something that you said concerning the 21st of October, 1993, that one of the BH army commanders said, "See you in Vares"?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said so, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I am not allowed to ask you about the legal qualifications or the legal definitions of civil war, but I can ask you the following as an officer: Do you know how civilians and soldiers were treated in the American civil war?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, relevance.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the question was misinterpreted. The question was interpreted as how civilians and soldiers were treated in the American civil war. The question was: What was the ratio between civilian and military casualties. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question is quite technical. Therefore, in the American civil war, what was the ratio between civilian casualties and military casualties?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I must agree with the Prosecutor. This is not a question for a witness who is here to tell what his experience was, what he has seen and heard in the connection with Vares. It's a question for an expert on American history. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, any senior officer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We're not going to discuss this. The Court rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, can you please move on to another question for the following reason: What took place during the civil war in the United States of America is something of a very complex nature, and the witness will probably not be in a position to shed any light on this for the Chamber, and we are very, very far from what -- from your case, from what is at the heart of your case. So intellectually speaking, yes, indeed that can be a very interesting question, but legally speaking it's irrelevant. That's why my fellow Judge has asked you to move on to a different topic. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Very well. There was this question that after World War I in any subsequent war there were more civilian than military deaths and the ratio was always negative.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But tell me the following: The communications systems you used between platoons and companies, did it require you to have a position on higher ground, or were your communication -- communications always operational also with the units that were stationed in valleys? My question, therefore, is: Did your communications system function at all times in and around Vares?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this time we have an operation -- I had one platoon in Kopjari area, and we have clear contact with radio contact from my company staff in Vares to this place. It was no problem. It was therefore -- also was informed of -- about the attack of Kopjari this morning, the 21st of October.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, I didn't mention Kopjari at all, and I did not mention the communications between Kopjari and Vares. My question to you was: At any point in time when your units were stationed in valleys were they able to communicate properly, given the layout of the terrain, or did you perhaps have difficulties in communicating with an APC or a platoon if it was in a depression. Did you have any such communications difficulties and, if so, which?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I agree with what you are saying. There was some problem with radio communications. So therefore we put up one platoon in Mijakovici. It's up in the area here, in the highest place north of -- of here. I think it's not on the map, but here, up in the mountains, we had one platoon. So we use this platoon also to say to Vares -- we use it for communications. Yes, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Right. So you had to have a platoon stationed on higher ground to use it as an intermediary for the purposes of communications; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions. Thank you, Lieutenant Colonel, for your exhaustive answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Birger, good morning to you. I am Defence counsel for General Petkovic, and I would like you to help us clarify some details in the documents shown to you by the Prosecutor today. I should also like us to examine some important details not only concerning the events at Stupni Do but in Vares in general. I would like to start with your diary which is contained in the Prosecution bundle under number 502980 [as interpreted]. Please look at the entry for the 25th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I will repeat the number P 02980. Now it's correct. On page 18 of the English version there is an entry for the 25th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. Please wait. I couldn't find 2980.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Are you looking at my set of documents or the Prosecutor's, because I was referring -- this is my set of documents. Please, I'm referring you to the Prosecutor's set of documents. The Prosecutor showed you 2980 today --

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: -- on page 18 of the English version, and page 15 of the version in the B/C/S. It's somewhere in the middle of the page, the last paragraph, which reads, and I will read it in English: "A telefax arrived from the command for the BH in Kiseljak with a copy of the order from the supreme HVO commander, General Petkovic, to the effect that the Bobovac Brigade should cooperate with UNPROFOR and that the mayor and the commander of the Bobovac Brigade were relieved of their duties." Did I read that part of the diary accurately, Mr. Birger?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us try to analyse this sentence together. Let me remind you that if something was entered in your diary under the date of the 25th of October, 1993, then what is stated there must have happened on that date. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- yes. If it's written in my diary, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It transpires from this sentence of yours that from the Kiseljak command you received a telefax; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember if it came directly from Kiseljak or if it's came from the battalion staff in Tuzla. What I could see in the document today, it was -- it was sent by fax from -- to, or inside the battalion. You could see NordBat 2 up in the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us try to analyse this sentence of yours and we will come to the documents later. Does it not transpire from this sentence of yours that you were delivered in the attachment a copy of General Petkovic's order?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please explain your question. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please look at the English text. The word "an," which is an indefinite article, and shows that you received one single order, because had you received several orders then it would not say "order," it would say "orders." And if we analyse the sentence linguistically, we can conclude that you received one single order by General Petkovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does it follow from this sentence of yours that this is an order ordering the Bobovac Brigade to cooperate with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
